item.title: Information Gaps and Riding the Wave
item.description:
Information asymmetry and leverage thinking are two of the most fundamental yet effective profit logics in business. They can be used separately or combined into a powerful strategy.

The essence of information asymmetry is simple: you know something others do not, or you can get that knowledge at a lower cost than they can. In practice, this is not about keeping secrets. It is about efficiency.

Leverage thinking means borrowing existing resources, channels, or results to lower your own cost of acquisition. No one has the bandwidth to explore every domain personally. Using others work is the rational choice.

Combining these two creates a powerful business strategy: use information asymmetry to identify value gaps, then use leverage to capture that value at minimal cost.

The practical path has three steps. First, build an information advantage: follow sources others ignore, organise data others leave scattered. Second, find leverage: identify proven models, tools, or channels and stand on shoulders. Third, convert: turn your information advantage into real economic returns.

This framework works because it respects a basic law of business: money is not made through brute force. It is made through structural advantages.

item.title: A Bank Teller Existential Crisis
item.description:
The first symptom of an existential crisis is a disturbance in the perception of time. When someone has sat at the same window for six years, time is no longer a linear river. It becomes an unmarked expanse of water.

At ten to nine in the morning, he puts on his uniform, fastens the buttons, and glances at the mirror in the changing room. The person in the mirror wears a navy blue suit with a badge on the lapel, his name and an employee number. He knows that in ten minutes, that number will matter more than his name. He walks to the counter, sits down, turns on the computer, enters his password. The system boots up. At nine oclock, the shutter rises. This is his sixth year at this bank, at this window.

In the beginning, everyaction felt fresh. Counting cash, checking signatures, authorisations, stamping. Everyaction had weight. By the sixth year, these movements had become muscle memory. He can process a transaction while thinking about what to have for dinner, his brain and bodycompletely separated. At the end of the day, he cannot remember a single transaction or a single face. Time has flowed through him like water, leaving no trace.

This is not just about repetitive work. Repetition does not necessarily lead to alienation. A craftsman repeats the same movements every day, but each repetition hassubtle differences and improvement. The bank teller predicament is different: his work has been designed to eliminate variation. Every process has been standardised. Every decision has been taken away from him. He is not required to judge, only to execute. He is not required to create, only to comply. He is not a service provider. He is an interface of the system.

The real crisis is not that the work istedious. It is that he knows, clearly, that the system is accelerating toward his obsolescence. ATMs eliminated seventy percent of teller positions. Mobile banking is eliminating the remaining thirty. Everything he does every day is being replaced line by line by code. He sits there not because the system needs him, but because the system is not quite ready to replace him yet.

That is when he started noticing small changes. During his lunch break, he takes a few extra minutes. At the end of the day, when balancing the books, he deliberately slows down. He is not slacking off. He is stretching the time during which he is still useful. In an almost imperceptible way, he is resisting the approaching nothingness.

item.title: A Programmer Complete Problem-Solving Framework
item.description:
The methodology that programmers develop through debugging and writing code can be applied to nearly every domain. It is not about syntax or specific frameworks. It is about a structured approach to defining, decomposing, and solving problems.

Step one is defining the problem. Programmers absolutely refuse to accept vague descriptions. They treat all I think,roughly, sort of statements as traps. The problem must be translated into measurable, verifiable indicators. The core actions are: restate the problem in your own words until the other person confirms it is correct, clarify the input, output, and constraints, and ask upfront what counts as solved and what does not. Solving the wrong problem is worse than not solving the problem at all.

Step two is decomposing the problem. When faced with any complex problem, the instinctive reaction is not how do I solve it, but how can I break it into several independent smaller problems. The criterion for decomposition is: mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive. How far do you break it down? Until each subproblem is simple enough to solve without thinking.

Step three is making a plan. Spend time planning before executing. Do not pursue a perfect solution in one pass. List all possible solutions, evaluate their pros and cons, choose the best one, and write down what to do first and what to do next. Planning time is always worth it.

Step four is hypothesis testing. This is what distinguishes average practitioners from experts. When faced with a problem, collect all phenomena and data, propose the most likely cause, design the smallest possible experiment to validate it, and continue or reject the hypothesis based on the results. The core of this method is rigour, not random guessing.

Step five is pattern recognition. Ninety-nine percent of the problems you encounter have already been encountered by someone else and have a mature solution. The first reaction to a problem should not be I will build it from scratch, but has someone already solved this?

Step six is the minimum viable product. Build a version that only preserves the core functionality, get the wholepipeline running, and then iterate based on feedback. Change only one thing at a time. Keep all historical versions so you can roll back at any time.

Step seven is exception handling. Programmers arenaturally pessimistic. They always assume the worst will happen. When designing a solution, they ask themselves: what if the user enters wrong data? What if the system crashes? The earlier a problem surfaces, the better.

Step eight is automation. Anyrepetitive manual operation should be replaced with a script or tool. One investment, permanent benefit.

item.title: The Rapid Development of Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
The rapid advancement of AI has a highly differentiated impact on different economies. For economies that occupy the lower-end of the technology chain and rely on large-scale labour as their engine, this impact first manifests as economic urgency.

Take parts of Southeast Asia as an example. Their past competitiveness did not come from technological advantage. It came from the scale and cost advantage of their labour force. This is a development path that compensates for efficiency through quantity. As AI increasingly replaces standardised intellectual and manual labour, the sustainability of this path is being fundamentally shaken.

For economies that do not fully price labour according to market forces, but instead maintain social structure by grading work through institutions and ideology, the challenge posed by AI is even more complex. It is not just an economic issue. It also involves social structure and ethical dilemmas. When large numbers of traditional jobs are replaced by AI, both theoriginal social stratification mechanism and the value distribution system face restructuring.

The impact of AI on the economy and society is not evenly distributed. Who benefits, who loses, and how they are affected depends on the structural characteristics of each economy. Understanding this non-uniform distribution is far more useful than simply judging whether AI is good or bad.

item.title: Data Asset Awareness
item.description:
Why are spreadsheets created by business development teams always messy? The answer is not carelessness or poor data literacy. It is a structural disconnect between the BD mindset and the standardisation required by data engineering.

For BD professionals, a spreadsheet is ascratchpad, not a structured database. Their core work logic is: chase clients, record information, track progress. The spreadsheet is just a tool for getting the job done, not a data asset that needs managing. This usage context means they will not spend time maintaining data standards, because the benefit they get from it is too small and the effort required is too large.

From a data asset perspective, this points to a deeper problem: when an organisation core data assets depend entirely on frontline employees self-discipline to maintain, the decline in data quality is inevitable. It is not a question of employee quality. It is a question of incentive structure. Maintaining data standards is a cost to employees and a benefit to the organisation. This mismatch between cost and benefit leads to the universal failure of data governance.

The solution is not to train employees on how to fill in spreadsheets properly. It is to change the way data is collected. Either automate the data collection process to reduce manual entry at source, or make the benefit of standardised entry flow back directly to the person filling in the form, instead ofall flow to the organisation.

Data asset awareness is never built through training. It is built through system design.

item.title: Fake It Till You Make It: Taking the First Step
item.description:
The logic of taking the first step runs counter to most people instinct. The first step is never about being ready.

You do not need to be highly professional, highly skilled, deeply knowledgeable, or vastly experienced. The first step requires only one thing: put it out there. List it on Xianyu. Your service is live. You are now in business.

The reality behind this logic is that the first step is not about demonstrating capability. It is about claiming a position. You do not need to be qualified before you enter the arena. You just need to show up first. Many doctors are not fully proficient when they start their jobs. They only truly learn after they have started.

Real-world capability growth is not linear. It is stepwise. You jump to the next level first, then learn to stand steady on that level. If you wait until you have learned everything before you jump, you will never learn, because real learning happens after action, not before.

This logic applies to every field. If you want to offer consulting services, list a service first, and learn by doing when someone buys. If you want to create content, publish a post first, and adjust based on feedback when someone reads it. If you want to build a product, ship a minimum viable version first, and iterate when someone uses it.

This has nothing to do with perfectionism or risk control. It is about a fundamental truth about learning pathways: the most effective learning model is action-driven learning, not learning-driven action.

Jump first. The parachute will open on the way down.

item.title: Excel Is Two-Dimensional
item.description:
Excel uses rows and columns because two-dimensional tables are the easiest structure for the human eye and brain to understand. But the real world is not two-dimensional.

Take mobile phone recycling as an example. The factors that affect the value of a single phone include at least a dozen dimensions: model, condition, battery, channel, time ofbuyback, weather, market sentiment, new product launches, inventory levels, profit margin, turnover days. These dimensions also interact with each other: weather affectsbuyback price, buyback price determines profit margin, profit margin relates to inventory strategy. Excel cannot naturally express this kind of multi-dimensional relational network.

At its core, the problem is that the human brain is not wired to process high-dimensional information, but computers are. Traditional software forces the high-dimensional world into a two-dimensional table so that humans can understand it. The data is still there, and the numbers are still there, but the relationships are broken and the patterns are invisible.

Systems like Palantir take the opposite approach. They do not flatten the data. They preserve the multi-dimensional network structure. All entities are treated as nodes, and all relationships between entities are treated as connections. The computer is responsible for storing andrelating all the dimensions. Humans only need to query when necessary.

Excel flattens the world so humans can see it. Palantir preserves the world as it is and lets the computer understand it.

The practical lesson for real business is this: when you need to make a decision based on multiple dimensions, do not try to cram everything into a single spreadsheet. Use a networked data structure to preserve the complete set of relationships. Your brain cannot simultaneously process a dozen dimensions, but a computer can store the relationships, find the patterns, and give you the answer.

item.title: Separating Business and Personal Accounts
item.description:
Running a business and creating content are not in conflict. In fact, they complement each other. This is not an either-or choice. It is a question of resource allocation.

From a logical perspective, these two paths not only avoid conflict, they reinforce each other.

Enterprise services target the B2B market: building software, solving problems for companies, earning money through professionalism and reliability, with stable income, high customer value, and strong repeat business. Content creation targets the C2C market: making videos, writing opinions, building a personal brand, earning through influence and reach.

These two paths serve completely different markets and customer bases. Therefore, there is no risk of customer confusion.

What truly needs to be considered is the allocation of energy and roles. Doing two things at once inevitably divides one focus. But viewed from another angle, these two activities can form a positive cycle. Content creation can become a channel for attracting enterprise clients. Enterprise service cases and insights can becomematerial for content creation. Many successful business influencers have walked this path.

The key is to find the ratio that suits you best. If you need stable cash flow, prioritise enterprise services and treat content creation as a side line. If you are in the accumulation phase, prioritise content and use enterprise services to maintain basic income. This ratio can be adjusted dynamically.

The worst approach is to choose neither because you cannot decide. Start moving, adjust along the way. That is far more effective than standing still and thinking.

item.title: Supply Is Strong, Demand Is Weak
item.description:
The core contradiction in the current economy is structural: supply exceeds effective demand. This is not absolute overcapacity across all industries, but a differentiated, squeezing imbalance.

Starting with consumer goods: manufacturing capacity across many sectors is ample. Daily necessities, home appliances, clothing, and ordinary industrial goods are in abundant supply, with prices trending downward and competition intensifying. But the problem is not on the supply side. It is that effective purchasing power cannot keep up. It is not that people do not need these goods. It is that their disposable income is shrinking and their consumption behaviour is contracting.

On the services side, the situation is equally visible. Too many people have piled into catering, advertising, marketing planning, and new media, while AI-driven substitution has driven down prices for freelance work. More shops open, but the general public spends less frequently, only splurging during holidays, leaving most days quiet.

If this structure continues to evolve, it forms a self-reinforcing cycle. AI and industry competition reduce white-collar incomes. Lower incomes mean less spending. Less spending means lower revenue for businesses. Lower revenue leads to further lay-offs. More lay-offs mean even lower incomes for more people. The end result is a peculiar state of affairs: goods are abundant, prices are not skyrocketing, but ordinary people feel their purchasing power shrinking.

Two common misconceptions need correcting. The first is that every industry is in oversupply. In reality, low-end homogeneous supply is indeed excessive, but high-end customised services, specialist healthcare and elderly care, and scarce technical roles remain in strong demand. The second is that a crisis will erupt overnight. In reality, this is a long, slow squeeze. Essential goods remain stable in supply, and there will not be the kind of large-scale collapse seen in classical economic crises.

The value of understanding this structure is that seeing the trend is more important than working harder in the wrong direction. In an environment where supply exceeds demand, the only way out of the rat race is to move toward higher value-added and scarcer offerings.

item.title: Zero-Sum Games, Arms Races, and Prisoner Dilemmas
item.description:
What people commonly call involution (neijuan) has several precise theoretical models in academic discourse. They explain the same phenomenon from different angles: everyone works harder, yet no one improves their position.

The most direct theory is the arms race. Two countries compete to build more weapons. One builds one hundred missiles, the other builds two hundred. The first builds three hundred more. In the end, both have exhausted their resources, but the balance of power has not changed. Apply this model to work and study: everyone works longer hours, pursues higher degrees, and collects more certificates, but relative rankings stay the same while absolute returns diminish.

The second theory is the prisoner dilemma. Each individual makes the rationally optimal choice for themselves, but when everyone does the same, the collective ends up worse off. Companies slash prices. Platforms burn cash on subsidies. Workers compete in a race of overtime. Everyone knows this is unsustainable, but no one dares to be the first to stop.

The third theory is the zero-sum game. In a market where the total size is fixed, one person gain is another person loss. When room for growth disappears, competition shifts from making the pie bigger to fighting over the existing pie. The most efficient players win, but overall welfare does not increase.

Together, these three theories paint a complete picture of involution. Understanding them is not about being pessimistic. It is about finding the breakthrough point. The real way out is never about working harder on the same track. It is about switching to a different track, moving fromfighting over existing share to creatingincremental growth, from zero-sum to positive-sum.

item.title: Fair Profit Is Not Greed
item.description:
There is a clear line between marking up and ripping someone off, but most people draw it in the wrong place. Charging ten times cost is not necessarily wrong, but charging nothing over cost means you are losing on yourself.

Many people have a fundamental misunderstanding about profit. They equate markup with immorality.

But this equation ignores a basic fact of business: reasonable profit is not exploitation. It is recognition of value and compensation for risk.

Something costs ten pounds and sells for a hundred. Looks greedy on the surface. But what you do not see is the full cost chain: acquisition cost, screening cost, trust cost, after-service cost, time cost, opportunity cost. Add all these up and they often far exceed the raw material price.

The real rip-off is not high margin. It is hiding information, making false promises, selling inferior goods at premium prices. If you price reasonably, deliver your service honestly, and your customers buy willingly, even if your margin is high, that is legitimate business.

Markets run on voluntary exchange. A customer paying your price means they have decided your service is worth at least that much. If you underprice yourself, you are actually breaking this market signal. Customers will not thank you for low prices. They will doubt your quality.

What should truly worry you is not reasonable profit being earned. It is reasonable profit being shamed out of existence. When good people are afraid to charge what they are worth, only scammers remain.

item.title: Social Experiment Reality Shows
item.description:
Locking real people in an enclosed space, throwing them a crisis scenario, and letting them solve problems using their genuine personalities, knowledge, and experience. This format has existed in television and experimental theatre for years, with severalmature models.

The most precise classification is social experiment reality show plus immersive group survival game. It combines three elements: real social identities, an enclosed space, and a crisis challenge. The participants real identities as academics, scientists, businesspeople, artists, etc. determine their behaviour under crisis, which is completely different from scripted performances.

There aremature examples both domestically and internationally. The classicinternational formats are Survivor and Big Brother, which, although they add competitive and voting mechanisms, share the core premise of putting people in an enclosed environment and observing theirgenuine reactions. Domestically, there are various workplace and entrepreneurship reality shows. Despite significant post-production scripting, the overall framework is similar.

The core appeal of this format is that real human nature under pressure reveals unpredictable richness. The details that no script can write, a person instinctive response in a critical moment, thesubtle shift in attitude between two people, the self-organising process of a group, these are the most compelling content.

To produce a viable version of this format, there are two key design elements. First, set up an initial crisis that has enough tension to make all participants take it seriously. Second, ensure the participants have sufficient diversity in background so that different knowledge structures and experiences can genuinely collide.

item.title: The DM-Only Phenomenon on Xiaohongshu
item.description:
Posts asking for recommendations on Xiaohongshu almost universally get replies saying DM me. On the surface, this looks like information opacity, but underneath it is a complete business logic and platform rule system.

From a business perspective, the essence of this behaviour is the commercialisation of information asymmetry. Giving an answer publicly means the value of that information instantly drops to zero. Keeping the answer behind a DM means the information can be priced, traded, and screened. Everyone who replies DM me is operating their own information asset.

From a platform rule perspective, the algorithm and content moderation of the public comment section also incentivise this behaviour. Leaving contact details publicly may trigger the platform sensitive word filter. Calling for a DM avoids this risk. At the same time, DM conversations move users into private traffic, reducing dependence on the platformtraffic.

From a user psychology perspective, public replies amount tounpaid contribution, while DM conversations can establish one-to-one trust. In scenarios that require deep communication, such as renting, job hunting, or consulting, DMs are not just a transaction method. They are also a screening mechanism. People who take the initiative to DM have more genuine needs and a higher probability of closing.

This phenomenon reveals the deep structure of the platform economy. The public area is used for exposure and traffic generation. The private space is used for conversation and closing deals. This is not a loophole in the rules. It is the underlying design logic of the platform. People who understand this logic are not exploiting aloophole. They are aligning their business with the structural characteristics of the platform.

item.title: Rent Extraction vs. Rent Creation in Regulation Theory
item.description:
Two types of intermediaries play fundamentally different roles in economic activity. One type creates value. The other distributes value. The criterion for distinguishing between the two defines how we understand the true source of value in markets.

Value-creating intermediaries, with Apple as the classic case, are characterised by thenovel integration of elements that could not previously be combined, creating products that did not previously exist. In Apple case, scattered elements such as ARM CPUs, touch technology, the iOS ecosystem, and the App Store were integrated into the iPhone, a product category that did not exist before. The definingcharacteristic of this type of entity is: without it, the corresponding new product would not exist. It has irreplaceable integration value.

Markup intermediaries, with real estate agents and insurance agents as classic cases, are characterised by adding an intermediate layer to existing transactions without changing the product or service itself. Real estate agents match buyers and sellers. Insurance agentsmarket existing insurance products. Neither creates anything new. Their definingcharacteristic is raising the cost of acquiring the original product or service without creating substantive value.

The method for distinguishing between the two is simple: after removing the intermediary, does the original product or value still exist, and how does the cost change? For the value-creating intermediary, removal means the new category still exists (smartphones continue to exist), but one innovator is missing. For the markup intermediary, removal means the original product or service still exists, and the acquisition cost is lower.

This original observation has a precise correspondence in the academic economics literature. In a 1987 paper, Fred McChesney defined these two types of behaviour as Rent Creation and Rent Extraction. Rent creation corresponds to positive value creation. Rent extraction corresponds to the meaningless division of existing value, fully aligning with the observation above.

This framework has a direct practical implication for business model design: when choosing a business model, ask yourself one question. When I am removed from the transaction, does the cost go up or down? If it goes down, you are extracting rent. If it goes up, you are creating value.

item.title: Three Core Corporate Governance Dilemmas
item.description:
Three common dilemmas in corporate governance all point to the same root cause: the mismatch between institutional design and human nature.

The first dilemma is perverse incentives. When a company has no reasonable workload boundaries or incentive mechanisms, the more an employee does, the more tasks they are given. Hard work is not rewarded; it is punished with more work. The result is a reverse incentive: those who work hard lose out, while those who coast are comfortable. Employees actively reduce their output and pretend to be busy, and overall efficiency declines.

The second dilemma is diffusion of responsibility. In large organisations, everyone feels responsible for only their small piece. When something goes wrong, it is no one person fault. The consequence is that everyone completes their own tasks, but the overall goal is not achieved.

The third dilemma is short-termism. The evaluation cycle determines behaviour. Quarterly reviews incentivise short-term numbers. Annual reviews cause long-term value to be systematically neglected. When everyone is chasing short-term metrics, the accumulation of long-term competitive advantage is systematically overlooked.

These three dilemmas share a common root: there is always a gap between what can be measured and what truly matters. Companies measure what is easy to measure, but what truly determines long-term success is hard to measure. This is the measurement paradox: you measure what people do, so people do what you measure, but what you measure is often not what you truly want.

The direction for resolving these dilemmas is not to design more sophisticated evaluation systems. It is to find a balance: use systems to guarantee minimum standards, and use culture and values to drive excellence.

item.title: Time Moves Fast and Slow at the Same Time
item.description:
Nearly every office worker experiences this split perception of time: the day flies by, yet every minute feels like it is dragging. There is a clear psychological mechanism behind this feeling.

From a psychological perspective, these two feelings have completely different causes.

Time feels fast when your brain is not truly processing anything. Meetings, replying to messages, filling forms, busywork, scrolling on your phone. None of these require deep thinking. Your brain is on autopilot. No memory anchors, so the day passes as if you have not lived it. Psychologists call this time numbness: repetitive, mechanical, thoughtless time passes fastest in our perception.

Time feels slow, paradoxically, when you are paying too much attention to it. When you stare at the clock, waiting for the day to end, calculating how much longer you have to sit there. Every second is amplified. Time is not moving slower; your density of time perception is higher.

Both feelings arise from the same root cause: the work itself is neither engaging enough to invest in nor avoidable enough to escape. Your brain switches between numbness and anxiety, creating the paradox. When you look back, the day evaporated; when you are in it, every minute is painful.

The way out is not changing your mindset. It is changing your work structure. When your work has clear challenges, perceptible progress feedback, and room for autonomy, your brain enters flow state. Time neither drags nor disappears.

Time itself does not change. What changes is your relationship with it.

item.title: Rock n Roll Is More Important Than Cannons
item.description:
If we use two sounds to metaphor the logic of social operation, cannons represent hard commands and rules, while rock n roll represents the impulse for expression and creation.

In a world of only cannons, all rules are fixed and unquestionable. People do not need to think; they only need to obey. Efficiency may be high, but the room for innovation is zero. In any system with only top-down commands and no bottom-up feedback, the system will eventually ossify.

Rock n roll represents an opposing force: questioning, expression, creation. It is not always right, but it provides diversity. Diversity is the fundamental guarantee that a system can adapt and survive when the environment changes.

From a logical perspective, cannons maintain order while rock n roll drives evolution. Order and evolution need to coexist. Without order, the system descends into chaos. Without evolution, the system becomes obsolete when the environment shifts. What is needed is a balance between the two, not one overwhelming the other, but leaving room for expression within the framework of order.

This framework applies to systems at different levels, from national governance to corporate management to personal growth. In any system, preserving a degree of uncontrollable, spontaneous, creative force is a necessary condition for the long-term health of the system.

Rock n roll is more important than cannons, not because it is more noble, but because in a rapidly changing world, the speed of evolution determines the probability of survival. And the raw material for evolution never comes from commands. It comes from expression.
